Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- River waters spread over highways and farms, towns and parks in Washington on Thursday, shutting down traffic on a 20-mile stretch of heavily traveled Interstate 5 between Seattle and Oregon and threatening the federal roadway north of Seattle. Rescue boats are sent out Wednesday in Pierce County, south of Seattle, Washington. "If you're trying to do commerce between Portland (Oregon) and Seattle, there is no way right now," said Bob Calkins, a spokesman for the Washington State Emergency Operations Center in Camp Murray, near Tacoma. "That's the major way into Washington state from Oregon." Flooding south of Seattle near Chehalis covered parts of I-5 with 30 inches of water, prompting its closure until at least Monday, state transportation officials said. And state and local roads were also victims of the water. "The problem is, the one real good detour is just as flooded," Calkins said. North of Seattle, a levee failure in Arlington brought the Stillaguamish River up to the edges of I-5, which remained open although some access ramps were closed, transportation officials said. The rain also caused Amtrak to suspend service between Seattle and Portland until Saturday, "with no alternative transportation," the rail line said Thursday on its Web site. iReport.com: Are you there? Share pics, video . Across the state, a number of rivers had crested, but flooded roads remained hazardous. The risk of landslides was high, leading to the closure of all passes across the Cascades, officials said. A meteorologist for the National Weather Service in Seattle said 15 inches of rain that began Monday had ended. The rainfall swept across virtually all of the state, but its biggest effects occurred along the western half of Puget Sound, Calkins said. The swollen Puyallup River threatened the city by the same name, but Loretta Cutter, sprang into action.  Watch how Washington copes with wicked weather » . The administrator of a group home and a longtime resident there helped evacuate 47 residents from the Valley Community Inn, a home for the mentally challenged and developmentally disabled, to a shelter at a nearby church. And she made sure her husband and a grandson left their one-story rambler house and got safely situated. "It's a situation you don't realize you are going to be in; it's always someone else," she said from the shelter at the Sunrise Baptist Church in Puyallup, a few miles east of Tacoma. "It was pretty traumatizing to all of us." Cutter is one of 40,000 western Washington state residents in at least 19 communities whom authorities asked to leave their homes Thursday amid heavy flooding along the region's rivers and streams. Only 260 of them sought shelter Wednesday night at the 39 shelters for people, Calkins said. In addition, seven livestock shelters and two pet shelters were set up, he said. Meanwhile, the torrential downpours of the past few days transformed Thursday into drizzle, common in western Washington, which typically gets less rainfall in any given year than does Miami. "It just drizzles every day, or so it seems, whereas in Miami, when it rains, it's a bellywasher," Calkins said. This week's flooding was worsened by a warm spell that melted up to 7 feet of snow that had fallen around Puget Sound, he said. Health authorities have issued occasional boil-water orders, but that's not what worries Calkins. "The larger issue is, as people go to their homes, they may be walking through floodwater that is contaminated by sewage," he said.

“It’s a situation you don’t realize you are going to be in; it’s always someone else,” she said from the shelter at Sunrise Baptist Church in Puyallup, a few miles east of Tacoma. “It was pretty traumatizing to all of us.”

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — On Thursday, overflowing rivers inundated roads, farmland, communities, and parks across Washington. The flooding halted travel along a 20-mile section of busy Interstate 5 between Seattle and Oregon and also endangered the federal highway north of Seattle. A day earlier, rescue boats had been deployed in Pierce County, south of Seattle.

Bob Calkins, spokesperson for the Washington State Emergency Operations Center at Camp Murray near Tacoma, said commercial travel between Portland, Oregon, and Seattle was effectively impossible. He noted that I-5 is the primary route into Washington from Oregon.

Near Chehalis, south of Seattle, floodwater reached 30 inches deep on portions of I-5. State transportation authorities said the highway would remain closed until at least Monday. State and local roads were flooded as well, including the only practical alternate route, according to Calkins.

Farther north, a breached levee in Arlington caused the Stillaguamish River to rise to the edge of I-5. The highway stayed open, although transportation officials closed several entrance and exit ramps.

The rain also led Amtrak to stop service between Seattle and Portland through Saturday. On its website Thursday, the rail operator said it would not provide substitute transportation.

iReport.com asked people in the area to submit photographs and video.

Although several rivers throughout Washington had already reached their highest levels, flooded roads continued to pose dangers. Officials also warned of a significant landslide threat and closed every mountain pass through the Cascades.

A National Weather Service meteorologist in Seattle said a storm that began Monday and produced 15 inches of rain had ended. Calkins said rain affected almost the entire state, with the most severe consequences occurring along the western side of Puget Sound.

The overflowing Puyallup River placed the city of Puyallup at risk, prompting longtime resident Loretta Cutter to act. Cutter, who manages a group home, helped move all 47 residents of the Valley Community Inn—a facility serving people with mental and developmental disabilities—to a shelter in a nearby church. She also ensured that her husband and grandson left their single-story rambler and reached safety.

Speaking from the shelter at Sunrise Baptist Church in Puyallup, several miles east of Tacoma, Cutter said people tend to think emergencies like this will happen to someone else, not to them. She described the experience as deeply traumatic for everyone involved.

Cutter was among roughly 40,000 residents in western Washington whom officials ordered or advised to leave their homes Thursday. The evacuations covered at least 19 communities affected by serious flooding along rivers and streams. Calkins said that only 260 people had stayed Wednesday night in the 39 shelters established for residents. Authorities also opened seven shelters for livestock and two for pets.

By Thursday, the torrential rain of the previous several days had eased into the light drizzle typical of western Washington. Despite its rainy reputation, the region generally receives less annual precipitation than Miami. Calkins contrasted Washington’s seemingly constant drizzle with Miami’s much heavier bursts of rain.

A period of warm weather intensified the flooding by melting as much as seven feet of snow that had accumulated around Puget Sound, Calkins said.

Public health agencies occasionally instructed residents to boil their water. However, Calkins said his greater concern was that people returning home might have to walk through floodwater polluted with sewage.
outputs.L3:
Severe flooding across Washington inundated highways, farms, towns, and parks, creating widespread transportation hazards and major disruptions. Near Chehalis, a 20-mile stretch of Interstate 5 was closed after floodwaters reached roughly 30 inches, cutting a crucial travel and commercial link between Seattle and Portland.

Farther north, a levee failure in Arlington caused the Stillaguamish River to surge toward I-5. Although the interstate remained open, several access ramps were closed as officials monitored rising water levels. Rail travel was also affected, with Amtrak suspending service between Seattle and Portland. Flooded detour routes and closures on Cascade mountain passes left travelers with few practical alternatives.

The flooding followed days of intense rainfall, with some areas receiving as much as 15 inches since Monday. Western Puget Sound experienced the most severe effects, while saturated ground across the region kept the risk of landslides dangerously high. Officials urged residents and travelers to avoid flooded roads, monitor emergency alerts, and prepare for continued disruptions.
outputs.L4:
Days of heavy rain drenched Washington, with some areas receiving as much as 15 inches. Rivers quickly spilled over their banks, flooding farms, highways, and low-lying towns and forcing officials to close roads and mountain passes across the state.

Emergency crews deployed rescue boats to reach stranded residents and motorists. Authorities urged people to avoid flooded roads, warning that fast-moving water could sweep away vehicles and that damaged pavement might be hidden beneath the surface. Rail service was also suspended in affected areas because of water and debris on the tracks.

Among the most serious disruptions was the closure of a roughly 20-mile stretch of Interstate 5, the main north-south highway linking Seattle and Portland. Floodwater covered portions of the roadway, leaving drivers to seek lengthy detours and interrupting the movement of freight between Washington and Oregon.

Other important routes remained threatened by rising rivers, landslides, and standing water. The closures isolated some communities and slowed deliveries, commuter traffic, and commercial shipments throughout the region.

Although the rain eventually eased, the danger did not immediately pass. Runoff continued to swell rivers, while transportation officials faced the task of inspecting highways, bridges, rail lines, and mountain routes for damage. Officials said travel and commerce could remain severely disrupted until floodwaters receded and key corridors were declared safe to reopen.

## Flooding forces evacuations, closes highways and disrupts rail service across western Washington

**SEATTLE —** Days of heavy rain have triggered widespread flooding across western Washington, forcing some residents to evacuate, closing major highways and suspending Amtrak service as officials warn of landslides and potentially contaminated floodwater.

Emergency crews have carried out rescues in low-lying communities where rivers spilled over their banks and water covered roads, homes and farmland. Authorities have urged people in evacuation zones to leave promptly and warned drivers never to attempt to cross flooded roadways.

Several highways and local roads have been shut down because of standing water, debris and unstable slopes. Transportation officials said conditions could change quickly and advised travelers to check official road updates before leaving.

Amtrak service through parts of western Washington has also been suspended because of flooding, debris and landslide concerns along the rail corridor. Passengers are being asked to contact Amtrak for rebooking and updated service information.

The prolonged rainfall has saturated hillsides throughout the region, increasing the risk of mudslides and falling trees even after the heaviest rain ends. Residents near steep slopes are being told to watch for warning signs such as cracking soil, leaning trees, unusual rumbling sounds or sudden changes in water flow.

Health officials are also warning people to avoid contact with floodwater, which may contain sewage, fuel, agricultural chemicals, sharp debris and bacteria. Anyone exposed should wash thoroughly with soap and clean water, while food, medicine and household items touched by floodwater should be discarded when they cannot be safely disinfected.

Officials say residents should continue monitoring evacuation notices, river forecasts, highway alerts and local emergency messages as floodwaters may remain high and additional closures are possible.

# Torrential rain inundates Washington communities as levees fail and roads close

**By [Reporter Name]**  
**Updated [time and date]**

**[CITY], Wash.** — Days of torrential rain triggered widespread flooding across parts of Washington on [day], forcing residents from their homes, closing major roads and overwhelming drainage systems as emergency crews responded to reports of levee failures and rising rivers.

Authorities opened shelters in [communities/counties] and urged people in low-lying areas to be prepared to evacuate. The most serious flooding was reported near [river or watershed], where [describe confirmed levee breach, overtopping or erosion]. Water entered [homes, businesses or farmland], and officials warned that conditions could deteriorate as runoff continued moving downstream.

Bob Calkins, an emergency spokesman for [agency or jurisdiction], said responders were prioritizing rescues, evacuations and access to isolated neighborhoods.

> “[Insert Calkins’ verified quotation about current conditions and the emergency response],” Calkins said. “[Insert verified quotation concerning evacuations, road travel or the expected duration of the flooding].”

Officials asked residents not to drive around barricades or attempt to cross flooded roads. Even shallow, fast-moving water can sweep away a vehicle, and pavement beneath floodwater may have collapsed or washed out.

## Shelters open for displaced residents

Emergency shelters were operating at [verified shelter names and addresses], with additional facilities on standby in [locations]. Authorities said the shelters were providing [cots, meals, drinking water, charging stations, pet accommodations or medical support, as confirmed].

Residents were advised to bring identification, essential medications, phone chargers, warm clothing and supplies for children. People with pets were told to check whether individual shelters accepted animals or whether separate facilities had been arranged.

[County or city] officials said transportation assistance was available by calling [verified number]. Anyone facing an immediate threat was advised to call 911.

At [location], resident Loretta Cutter said the water rose [verified description of timing and depth], leaving [her home, street or neighborhood] surrounded.

> “[Insert Cutter’s verified quotation describing what she saw and how the flooding affected her],” Cutter said. “[Insert a second verified quotation about evacuation, property damage or community conditions].”

## Roads blocked by water, slides and debris

Flooding, standing water, fallen trees and landslides disrupted travel across the region. [State routes, highways and local roads] were closed or restricted near [locations], according to [Washington State Department of Transportation/local agency].

Transportation officials warned that closure information could change quickly. Drivers were urged to consult the Washington State Department of Transportation’s real-time travel map and local emergency alerts before leaving home.

Crews were inspecting bridges, culverts and roadbeds for erosion. Some routes could remain closed after water recedes because floodwater can undermine pavement and destabilize slopes.

Rail, ferry or public-transit service in [area] was [suspended, delayed or operating normally], according to [confirmed source].

## Levee failures intensify flooding threat

The flooding worsened after [a levee failed/several levees overtopped/a protective embankment was damaged] near [location], sending water into [neighborhoods, industrial areas or agricultural land]. Officials established an evacuation zone covering [verified boundaries].

Engineers and public-works crews were monitoring other levees for seepage, erosion and structural movement. Authorities warned residents not to approach damaged flood-control structures, where currents can be powerful and the ground unstable.

It was not immediately clear [how many structures were damaged/whether repairs could begin before water levels fell]. [Responsible agency] said it would assess the levee once conditions allowed.

## Contaminated water and other health risks

Health officials warned that floodwater may contain sewage, fuel, agricultural chemicals, sharp debris and bacteria. Residents were advised to avoid contact whenever possible and to keep children and pets away.

Anyone exposed to floodwater should wash with soap and clean water, cover open cuts and seek medical advice if a wound becomes red, swollen or painful. Food, medicine and cosmetics touched by floodwater should generally be discarded.

Officials also issued [a boil-water advisory/do-not-drink notice] for [confirmed service area] after [loss of pressure or possible contamination]. Residents there were instructed to use bottled water or follow the precise guidance issued by their water provider.

People returning to flooded buildings were warned about electrical hazards, unstable walls, mold and carbon-monoxide poisoning. Generators, grills and camp stoves should never be used inside homes, garages or other enclosed spaces.

## More rain possible

The National Weather Service said [verified amount] of rain had fallen in [location] over [time period], with another [forecast amount] possible through [time]. [Flood watches/warnings] remained in effect for [counties, rivers or communities].

Forecasters said rivers could continue rising even after the heaviest rain ended because water was still draining from saturated hillsides and mountain watersheds.

Officials urged residents to sign up for local emergency notifications, keep phones charged and be ready to leave immediately if ordered.
